source_text: CAPUT SEPTIMUM, De resurrectione carnis. Habita de fine hujus mundi disputatione stabilis: sequitur resurrectio carnis, quae est nova, inseparabilis & definitiva animarum, quotquot a corporibus suis per mortem abscesserunt, cum iisdem illis corporibus unio, futura supremo hujus saeculi die, potentia & jussu Dei, ut unusquisque tribunali Christi judicis Deo sistatur & congruenter ad id, quod fecerit, reportet sive bonum, sive malum sempiternum.
english: CHAPTER SEVEN. On the resurrection of the flesh.

The disputation concerning the end of this world having been settled: there follows the resurrection of the flesh, which is a new, inseparable, and definitive union of souls — as many as have departed from their bodies by death — with those same bodies, future on the last day of this age, by the power and command of God, so that each one may be presented before the tribunal of Christ the judge to God and may carry away, correspondingly to what he has done, either everlasting good or everlasting evil.

source_text: IV. Caeterum, quicquid Democritus, quem Plinius ridet lib. 7. cap. 55. vel ejusdem farinae alii de resurrectione balbutiverunt, id totum nonnisi fando accepisse potuerunt, sive e traditione, quam tamen ut plurimum vel corruptam a doctoribus suis acceperunt, vel corruperunt ipsi: e ratione vero seu principiis, quae citra revelationem nota omnes admitterent, haurire non potuerunt. Nullum enim eorum est, e quo liceat evincere, resurrectionem corporum aliquando futuram esse.
english: IV. For the rest, whatever Democritus — whom Pliny mocks (Natural History book 7, chapter 55) — or others of the same flour stammered concerning resurrection, they could have received that whole only by hearsay, either from tradition, which yet for the most part they either received corrupt from their teachers or themselves corrupted: but from reason or from principles which all would admit as known apart from revelation they could not draw it. For there is none of those from which it is permitted to prove that the resurrection of bodies will sometime be future.

source_text: Hi tamen authores Josepho Acosta supra a nobis laudato contradicunt. Quod si quicquam de resurrectione a barbaris creditum fuit, id ad eos traditione & quasi per manus a majoribus delatum fuisse, sicuti opinio de diluvio, quod nequidem ipsum penitus incognitum fuit, statuendum est. Vide notas ad Benzonis libri 1. caput 10. Et vero si cognitionem horum talium mysteriorum non alio referimus, quam ad traditiones majorum: minus certe mirum est, Senecam epist. 36. ad resurrectionem alludere. Et quid a Christiano de resurrectione disertius & rectius diceretur, quam quod Phocylidae transcribitur. Quod carmen Josephus Scaliger animadversionibus Eusebianis num. 1480. non illius antiquissimi Phocylidae esse statuit, sed Hellenistae cujusdam Alexandrini, aut, quod vero propius existimat, alicujus Christiani. Eusebius quoque lib. 11. praeparationis Euangelicae cap. 11. suadere conatur, Platoni resurrectionem mortuorum cognitam fuisse: sed probabilius est, eum non tam ad resurrectionem nobis creditam, quam ad τὴν παλιγγενεσίαν & ἀποκατάστασιν, qualem magno sub anno exacto Platonici comminiscuntur, allusisse.
english: Yet these authors contradict Joseph Acosta, praised by us above. But if anything concerning resurrection was believed by the barbarians, it is to be established that it was handed down to them by tradition and as it were by hand from the ancestors, just as the opinion concerning the flood, which was not itself utterly unknown. See the notes on Benzoni book 1, chapter 10. And indeed if we refer knowledge of such mysteries to nothing other than the traditions of the ancestors, it is certainly less wonderful that Seneca in letter 36 alludes to resurrection. And what would be said by a Christian concerning resurrection more expressly and rightly than what is transcribed under Phocylides' name? Which poem Joseph Scaliger in the Eusebian Animadversions number 1480 judged not to be of that most ancient Phocylides, but of some Alexandrian Hellenist, or — what he thinks nearer the truth — of some Christian. Eusebius also (Preparation for the Gospel book 11, chapter 11) tries to persuade that the resurrection of the dead was known to Plato: but it is more probable that he alluded not so much to the resurrection believed by us as to the παλιγγενεσία and ἀποκατάστασις such as the Platonists invent when the great year is completed.

source_text: Sacra scriptura enim nos ducit longius eo quo lumen rationis non potest. Docet enim hanc immortalem animam suo iterum corpori aliquando junctum iri, & ipsum quoque corpus immortalitatis fore particeps: quod nihil aliud est, quam resurrectio carnis sive illius ipsius corporis, a quo olim anima abscessit, quod a vermibus consumtum, vel in cineres redactum, vel quovis alio casu & modo corruptum fuit: quam tanquam articulum fidei nostrae in Apostolico aliisque catholicis symbolis credere nos Christiani profitemur.
english: For Sacred Scripture leads us further than where the light of reason can. For it teaches that this immortal soul will sometime again be joined to its body, and that the body itself also will be partaker of immortality: which is nothing other than the resurrection of the flesh, or of that very body from which the soul formerly departed, which has been consumed by worms, or reduced to ashes, or corrupted by any other chance and mode — which we Christians profess to believe as an article of our faith in the Apostles' Creed and in the other catholic symbols.

source_text: II. Dico autem unionem novam, quia anima, quae jam olim, cum generatur homo, unita fuerat corpori, & ab eo per mortem separata nunc denuo unitur. Inseparabilem dico, quia nunquam iterum separabitur, sed in aeternum unita permanebit; cum circa eos, qui a Christo, prophetis & Apostolis resuscitati sunt, nova quidem unio facta fuerit, sed quae per mortem iterum dissolvebatur. III. Disquiri autem potest, cum de resurrectione carnis articulus fidei Christianae pure & proprie dicatur, unde sit, quod illius etiam in animis & opinionibus gentium vestigia quaedam observentur? Ariovistus enim & Germani apud Appianum libro de bellis Gallicis dicuntur θανάτου καταφρονηταὶ ἐπ' ἐλπίδι ἀναβιώσεως, mortis contemptores propter spem vitae recuperandae. Quin etiam de barbaris Americanis referunt nonnulli, resurrectionis aliquem sensum habuisse. Hispanos enim, qui ut opibus, quas cum funeribus defodi solitas superius diximus, potirentur, sepulchris apertis ossa disturbabant, a Peruanis rogatos esse, ne facerent, quod resurrectioni forte obesse posset.
english: II. But I call the union new, because the soul, which formerly when a human is generated had been united to the body and separated from it by death, is now again united. I call it inseparable, because it will never again be separated but will remain united forever — whereas concerning those who were raised by Christ, the prophets, and the Apostles, a new union indeed was made, but one which was again dissolved by death.

III. But it can be asked, since the article of Christian faith concerning the resurrection of the flesh is said purely and properly, whence it is that certain vestiges of it are also observed in the minds and opinions of the nations? For Ariovistus and the Germans in Appian On the Gallic Wars are said to be despisers of death because of hope of recovering life. Indeed some also report concerning the American barbarians that they had some sense of resurrection. For the Spaniards, who that they might possess the riches customarily buried with funerals — as we said above — disturbed bones with opened tombs, were asked by the Peruvians not to do what might perhaps hinder the resurrection.
